items.title: The Antidote to Restlessness: Nine Stages of Settling, and Neither Rejoicing Nor Grieving

items.zh: 此蓋誰為非食？答：有奢摩他、及於彼相如理作意多所修習，以為非食。奢摩他者，謂九種住心，及奢摩他品所攝諸法。謂於自他若衰若盛可厭患法心生厭離，驚恐惡賤，安住寂靜。問：
items.en: What starves this hindrance? Answer: Calm-abiding, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. Calm-abiding is the nine stages of settling the mind, together with the various practices belonging to calm-abiding. This is towards whatever, in oneself or another, counts as decline or as prosperity, both being causes for genuine dismay: the mind grows dispassionate towards them, wary of the one, disinclined towards the other, and settles instead into genuine stillness.

items.title: What Feeds Doubt: Speculating About Self, Other Beings, and the Nature of the World

items.zh: 疑蓋以何為食？答：有去來今，及於彼相不正思惟多所修習，以之為食。謂我於過去為有？為無？廣說如上。不正思惟者，謂不可思處所攝思惟。不可思處者，謂我思惟、有情思惟、世間思惟。
items.en: What feeds the hindrance of doubt? Answer: The past, future, and present, together with sustained unsound reflection on them, are its food — was I, in the past, existent or not, and so on as explained at length elsewhere. Unsound reflection is reflection belonging to what should not be reflected on at all. What should not be reflected on is speculation about the self, about other beings, and about the world.

items.zh: 若於自處，依世差別思惟我相，名我思惟。若於他處，名有情思惟。若於有情世間及器世間處，名世間思惟。謂世間常、或謂無常、亦常亦無常、非常非無常等。問：
items.en: Speculating about one's own self across the differences of time is called speculation about the self. Doing the same regarding another is called speculation about other beings. Speculating about the world of sentient beings and the physical world itself — whether the world is permanent, impermanent, both, or neither, and so on — is called speculation about the world.

items.title: What Starves Doubt: Understanding Dependent Origination — and the Five Hindrances Close

items.zh: 此蓋誰為非食？答：有緣緣起、及於彼相如理作意多所修習以為非食。由彼觀見唯有於法及唯法因，唯有於苦及唯苦因故，所有一切不正思惟為緣無明，於三世境未生者不生，已生者能斷。
items.en: What starves this hindrance? Answer: Dependent origination with its conditions, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. Because such a practitioner sees clearly that there are only phenomena and the cause of phenomena, only suffering and the cause of suffering, the ignorance conditioning every kind of unsound reflection is, regarding the three times, prevented from arising where not yet arisen, and severed where already arisen.

items.zh: 若不如理而強作意，其如理者而不作意；總說此二名不正思惟。若於是中，應合道理，應知是處名為如理。
items.en: Forcibly attending to what is not appropriate, and not attending to what is appropriate: these two together are called incorrect reflection. Wherever something accords with reason, that should be understood as appropriate.

items.zh: 謂於闇中作光明想。由此方便如理作意，非不如理。於餘處所、亦有所餘如理作意。
items.en: That is, forming the perception of light within darkness. By this method, the reflection is sound, not unsound. And in every other case, there is likewise its own appropriate sound reflection.

items.title: The First Dhyāna's Five Qualities: Method, Benefit, and Essence Working Together

items.zh: 復次，於初靜慮具足五支。一、尋，二、伺，三、喜，四、樂，五、心一境性。
items.en: Further, the first dhyāna is fully endowed with five qualities: first, applied thought; second, sustained thought; third, joy; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind.

items.title: The Remaining Three Dhyānas: Inner Clarity, the Swimmer Fully Submerged, and Purified Stillness

items.zh: 第二靜慮有四支。一、內等淨，二、喜，三、樂，四、心一境性。第三靜慮有五支。一、捨，二、念，三、正知，四、樂，五、心一境性。第四靜慮有四支。一、捨清淨，二、念清淨，三、不苦不樂受，四、心一境性。
items.en: The second dhyāna has four qualities: first, inner clarity; second, joy; third, bliss; fourth, one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna has five qualities: first, equanimity; second, mindfulness; third, clear comprehension; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind. The fourth dhyāna has four qualities: first, purified equanimity; second, purified mindfulness; third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; fourth, one-pointedness of mind.

items.title: Why These Particular Qualities: Object, Support, and Enjoyment

items.zh: 初靜慮中，尋伺為取所緣，三摩地為彼所依，喜為受境界，樂為除麁重。第二靜慮中，內等淨為取所緣，三摩地為彼所依，餘如前說。第三靜慮中，捨、念、正知為取所緣，三摩地為彼所依，餘如前說。第四靜慮中，捨淨、念淨為取所緣，三摩地為彼所依，餘如前說。
items.en: In the first dhyāna, applied and sustained thought are what take hold of the object; concentration is what all of this rests on; joy is the experienced benefit; bliss is what removes coarse unfitness. In the second dhyāna, inner clarity is what takes hold of the object; concentration is what this rests on; the rest is as already explained. In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are what take hold of the object; concentration is what this rests on; the rest is as already explained. In the fourth dhyāna, purified equanimity and purified mindfulness are what take hold of the object; concentration is what this rests on; the rest is as already explained.

items.zh: 諸靜慮中雖有餘法，然此勝故，於修定者為恩重故，偏立為支。
items.en: Although other factors are genuinely present within each of these meditative absorptions, it is specifically these that are most excellent, and of the greatest benefit to the practitioner cultivating concentration — this is why these alone are singled out and established as each absorption's own defining qualities.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，初靜慮中有尋有伺耶？答：由彼能厭患欲界，入初靜慮，初靜慮中而未能觀尋伺過故。
items.en: Question: For what reason is the first dhyāna accompanied by initial and sustained thought? Answer: Because one enters the first dhyāna by becoming disenchanted with the desire realm, and in the first dhyāna one is not yet able to see the faults of initial and sustained thought.

items.title: Each Level Named for the Fault It Sees in the One Before

items.zh: 第二靜慮能觀彼過，是故說為尋伺寂靜。如第二靜慮見彼過故，名尋伺寂靜；如是第三靜慮見喜過故，名喜寂靜；第四靜慮見樂過故、名樂寂靜。捨念清淨，差別應知。
items.en: The second dhyāna is able to observe that fault, and is therefore called stilled of applied and sustained thought. Just as the second dhyāna, seeing that fault, is called stilled of thought, so the third dhyāna, seeing joy's own fault, is called stilled of joy; and the fourth dhyāna, seeing bliss's own fault, is called stilled of bliss. Purified equanimity and mindfulness, too, should be understood to differ in depth from level to level.

items.title: Two More Names for the Dhyānas: "Elevated Mind," and Why Only These Four Count as "Dwelling in Happiness"

items.zh: 復次，是諸靜慮名差別者，或名增上心。謂由心清淨增上力正審慮故。或名樂住。謂於此中受極樂故。所以者何？依諸靜慮領受喜樂、安樂、捨樂身心樂故。
items.en: Further, these dhyānas have further names as well. They are called "elevated mind," because it is through the elevating power of a purified mind that correct, careful examination becomes possible. They are called "dwelling in happiness," because within them one experiences the most complete happiness — resting on these absorptions, one experiences the happiness of joy, of ease, and of equanimity, a happiness of both body and mind together.

items.zh: 又得定者於諸靜慮數數入出，領受現法安樂住故。由此定中現前領受現法樂住。從是起已，作如是言：我已領受如是樂住。於無色定無如是受，是故不說彼為樂住。
items.en: Further, one who has attained concentration repeatedly enters and exits these absorptions, thereby experiencing this happiness, present and immediate, again and again. The formless attainments carry no such experience, which is why they are never called "dwelling in happiness."

items.title: Why a Realised Practitioner Must Say So When Asked, and Two Names Marking Absorption's Real Limits

items.zh: 然彼起已，應正宣說。何以故？若有阿練若苾芻來就彼問，彼若不答，便生譏論：此阿練若苾芻云何名為阿練若者，我今問彼超色無色寂靜解脫，而不能記。是故為說應入彼定，非為樂住。
items.en: Yet, having arisen from that attainment, one should rightly declare it. Why? Because if a forest-dwelling monastic comes and asks, and one does not answer, criticism follows: "How can this forest-dweller be called such, when I asked about the peaceful liberation transcending form and formlessness, and no answer could be given?" This is why one should explain: that absorption is to be entered, but it is not a dwelling in happiness.

items.zh: 或復名為彼分涅槃，亦得說名差別涅槃。由諸煩惱一分斷故，非決定故，名彼分涅槃。非究竟涅槃故，名差別涅槃。
items.en: They are also called "nirvāṇa in semblance," and may likewise be called "provisional nirvāṇa." Because only a portion of affliction is thereby severed, and not with any final certainty, they are called nirvāṇa in semblance. Because this is not ultimate nirvāṇa, they are called provisional nirvāṇa.

blocks.text: Today completes the five hindrances and then describes the four dhyānas by their factors. If you meditate, you will recognise the progression: each dhyāna is reached by seeing a fault in the one before.

Restlessness is starved by **calm** (止, *śamatha*): nine stages of settling the mind (described in detail in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*), and a mind that neither rejoices at prosperity nor grieves at decline. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that, for a practitioner, even prosperity is something to weary of, since wealth breeds heedlessness. His example is Devadatta, whose downfall began with Ajātaśatru's lavish offerings.

subs.head: Doubt: fed by speculation, starved by dependent origination

blocks.text: Doubt is fed by speculation about "self, other beings, and the world": are they permanent, impermanent, both, neither? It is starved by seeing "only dharmas and their cause, only suffering and its cause". Master Cháng Bǎi: in the twelve links, the first seven are "dharmas with a cause"; craving through old age and death are "suffering with a cause". Dependent origination (fascicles 9–10) is the cure for doubt, because it replaces speculation about essences with observation of conditions.

The **first dhyāna** has five factors: applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness. The treatise explains their roles: thought takes hold of the object; concentration is the support; joy is the experienced benefit; bliss removes coarse unfitness of body and mind (Day 7's coarse burden).

The **second dhyāna** has inner clarity (內等淨), joy, bliss, and one-pointedness. Master Cháng Bǎi: applied thought, so useful for leaving desire, is now dust that clouds the mind, and is shaken off. The **third dhyāna** has equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and one-pointedness. Master Cháng Bǎi's image again: joy is swimming with your head above water; bliss is being fully submerged. The **fourth dhyāna** has purified equanimity, purified mindfulness, neutral feeling, and one-pointedness.

subs.head: Each named for the fault it sees

blocks.text: "Just as the second dhyāna, seeing the fault of thought, is called stilled of thought, so the third, seeing joy's own fault, is called stilled of joy", and the fourth, seeing bliss's fault, is stilled of bliss. Progress in meditation is a series of renunciations of increasingly refined pleasures.

The dhyānas are called "**elevated mind**" (增上心), the second of the three trainings. Master Cháng Bǎi: 增上 means both "leading higher" and "supreme"; "if the mind isn't still, wisdom is a candle in the wind." Only the four dhyānas are called "**dwelling in happiness here and now**", because they bring happiness of body and mind; the formless attainments bring only mental ease.

The dhyānas are also called "**partial nirvāṇa**" (彼分涅槃). Both teachers, following Kuījī, explain 彼分 as "resembling": no affliction is active, so the state resembles nirvāṇa slightly. But resemblance is not identity; Day 51's error was to take it for the real thing.

quiz.q: Calm starves restlessness; the mind wearies of decline and prosperity alike. Why does Venerable Miào Jìng call wealth itself something to weary of?
options: for a practitioner, wealth breeds heedlessness — like Devadatta, who received five hundred carts of offerings from Ajātaśatru and went to hell
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "From the practitioner's standpoint, getting rich is also something to weary of — once rich, what happens? Heedlessness"; "Devadatta received five hundred carts of food from King Ajātaśatru, honoured and supported — and later went to hell."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what three matters "should not be reflected on" and feed doubt?
options: speculation about self, other beings, and the world
quiz.why: "What should not be reflected on is speculation about the self, about other beings, and about the world" — permanent, impermanent, both, neither. Master Cháng Bǎi: such probing cuts no afflictions, and too much of it makes one doubt whether one can practise at all.

quiz.q: Doubt is starved by seeing "only dharmas and their cause, only suffering and its cause." What are "dharmas" and their "cause," per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: the first seven links, ignorance through feeling, are "dharmas with a cause"; craving through old age-death are "suffering with a cause"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Of the twelve links, the first seven — ignorance through feeling — are 'dharmas with a cause'; craving through old age and death are 'suffering with a cause.'" Venerable Miào Jìng: 有緣 means having all four conditions. The translation doesn't convey this.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what five factors does the first dhyāna possess?
options: joy, bliss, equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension
inner clarity, joy, bliss, concentration, equanimity
applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, one-pointedness
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna is fully endowed with five qualities: first, applied thought; second, sustained thought; third, joy; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind." Master Cháng Bǎi: one-pointedness is the essence on which the antidote and benefit factors rest.

quiz.q: Master Cháng Bǎi uses a swimming image to contrast joy and bliss. How?
options: joy is like swimming with the head still above water; bliss is being fully submerged, body and mind wholly happy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Joy is like swimming with the head still above water; bliss is the whole body immersed — body and mind deeply happy in the water." So the third dhyāna drops joy and keeps bliss. Venerable Miào Jìng: in the third, the second's joy is discarded.

quiz.q: Why is the third dhyāna called "stilled of joy"?
options: it sees joy's fault — as the second, seeing thought's fault, is stilled of thought, and the fourth, seeing bliss's fault, is stilled of bliss
quiz.why: "Just as the second dhyāna, seeing that fault, is called stilled of thought, so the third dhyāna, seeing joy's own fault, is called stilled of joy." Master Cháng Bǎi: in the first dhyāna one can't yet see that applied thought is disturbing.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why are the formless attainments never called "dwelling in happiness"?
options: they lack such experience — the dhyānas give bodily and mental happiness, the formless only mental
quiz.why: "Resting on these absorptions, one experiences the happiness of joy, of ease, and of equanimity, a happiness of both body and mind … The formless attainments carry no such experience, which is why they are never called dwelling in happiness." Master Cháng Bǎi: the formless have only mental happiness.
